summary: Specifies how to encapsulate IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies on FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 1188.

plainLanguage.summary: FDDI is a ring of glass cables. This tells computers how to wrap their Internet packets so they ride around that ring.

subtitle: How to send IP packets and address resolution over fiber-optic token rings

tldr.problem: FDDI networks are high-speed token-ring networks using fiber optics, but they need a standard way to carry IP datagrams and ARP resolution over them.
tldr.mechanism: IP datagrams and ARP messages are wrapped in IEEE 802.2 LLC and SNAP headers before being sent as FDDI frames. Each frame includes FDDI MAC and physical layer framing, and address resolution is performed using standard ARP.
tldr.outcome: This standard enabled interoperable IP networking over FDDI. It was replaced by RFC 1188, which provided updated specifications.

today: RFC 1103 specifies IP transmission over FDDI networks and was on the standards track. It was superseded by RFC 1188, which provides updated specifications. FDDI networks were popular in the 1990s for high-speed LAN backbones but are largely obsolete today, replaced by faster technologies like Fast Ethernet and Gigabit Ethernet.

sections.title: Introduction to FDDI Networks
sections.content:
RFC 1103 specifies how to transmit Internet Protocol (IP) datagrams and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) requests and replies over Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) networks. FDDI is a family of standards for high-speed Local Area Networks that operates at the physical and media access control layers of the Data Link Layer.

FDDI networks form a token-passing ring topology with fiber-optic cables, providing speeds much higher than earlier technologies like Ethernet. The specification defines standards for the Media Access Control (MAC) layer, Physical layer protocol (PHY), Physical layer medium dependent (PMD), and Station Management (SMT).

The goal of this specification is to allow compatible and interoperable implementations for transmitting IP datagrams and ARP messages over FDDI, using the existing IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) service for data link operations. The stack of services is: IP/ARP, IEEE 802.2 LLC, FDDI MAC, FDDI PHY, and FDDI PMD.
sections.plainLanguage: FDDI is a very fast network that uses glass fiber cables in a ring shape. This memo shows how to make Internet packets work on FDDI by wrapping them in special headers.

sections.title: Packet Encapsulation and Formats
sections.content:
IP datagrams and ARP messages sent on FDDI networks must be encapsulated within the 802.2 LLC and Sub-Network Access Protocol (SNAP) data link layers and the FDDI MAC and physical layers. The SNAP header must use an Organization Code of zero, with the remaining 16 bits containing the EtherType code (2048 for IP, 2054 for ARP).

All frames must be transmitted in standard 802.2 LLC Type 1 Unnumbered Information format. The DSAP (Destination Service Access Point) and SSAP (Source Service Access Point) fields of the 802.2 header must both be set to the assigned global SAP value for SNAP, which is 170 decimal (0xAA in hexadecimal, or 10101010 in binary). The LLC control field value is 3 (Unnumbered Information), and the Protocol ID/Organization Code is 0.

The total length of the combined LLC Header and SNAP header is 8 octets. This structure allows FDDI to carry Ethernet-compatible frames, with the EtherType field indicating whether the payload is IP or ARP.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet packets get wrapped in special headers that label them with a code number. IP packets get 2048, ARP packets get 2054. All packets follow the same wrapping rules.

sections.title: Address Resolution and Hardware Parameters
sections.content:
The mapping of 32-bit Internet addresses to FDDI hardware addresses must be done via the standard Address Resolution Protocol (ARP). Each host's implementation must know its own Internet address and respond to ARP requests appropriately. It must also use ARP to translate Internet addresses to FDDI addresses when sending to other hosts.

For ARP on FDDI networks, the protocol uses hardware type code 6 (assigned for IEEE 802 networks, which FDDI networks use for ARP purposes even though FDDI is not strictly IEEE 802). The protocol type code for IP is 2048. FDDI addresses can be either 16-bit or 48-bit; the hardware address length in ARP is 2 for 16-bit addresses or 6 for 48-bit addresses. The protocol address length for IP is always 4 octets. ARP operation codes are 1 for request and 2 for reply. The broadcast Internet address (with all host bits set to one) must be mapped to the broadcast FDDI address (all bits set to one).
sections.plainLanguage: To find the glass cable address for an Internet address, computers ask each other using ARP, just like on Ethernet. FDDI addresses can be either 2 or 6 bytes long.

sections.title: Packet Size, MTU, and MAC Layer Details
sections.content:
The FDDI MAC specification defines a maximum frame size of 9000 symbols (4500 octets) for all frame fields, including preamble and delimiters. The MAC layer overhead includes a 2-octet preamble, 1-octet start delimiter, 1-octet frame control, 6-octet destination address (or 2-octet for 16-bit addressing), 6-octet source address (or 2-octet), 4-octet frame check sequence (FCS), and 2-octet end delimiter/frame status field. This leaves approximately 4470 octets (or 4478 with 16-bit addressing) available for data after subtracting the 8-octet LLC/SNAP header, giving a maximum packet size (MTU) of 4470 octets.

Gateway implementations must be prepared to accept full-length packets and fragment them when necessary. Host implementations should accept full-length packets but must not send datagrams longer than 576 octets unless they have explicit knowledge that the destination can accept them. FDDI networks may have larger MTUs than the default 576-octet Internet maximum, so hosts should be aware this could lead to fragmentation at downstream routers.

FDDI MAC also defines Frame Copied (C) and Address Recognized (A) indicators that provide information about successful delivery. If the Address Recognized bit is set but Frame Copied is reset, the destination is congested. If both are reset, the frame was not received; implementations should either ignore the error, send an ICMP message, or delete the ARP entry and try again.
sections.plainLanguage: FDDI frames can be up to 4470 bytes of actual data, much bigger than Ethernet. But Internet hosts usually send smaller packets unless they know the other end can take them.

sections.title: MAC Layer Requirements and Address Sizes
sections.content:
FDDI supports both 16-bit and 48-bit station addresses, but the MAC specification does not require that 16-bit and 48-bit address stations fully interwork. However, all 16-bit stations must have full 48-bit functionality, and both types must receive frames sent to either size broadcast address. For IP and ARP, all communicating stations on a LAN must use consistent address sizes. Implementations must discard any IP or ARP packets received with an unimplemented or inactive address size. If 16-bit and 48-bit implementations need to coexist and interwork, they must be treated as separate IP networks and linked with an IP router that supports both address sizes.

FDDI defines asynchronous and synchronous frame classes. Only asynchronous frames and unrestricted tokens are required for basic FDDI interoperability. All IP and ARP frames must be transmitted as asynchronous frames using unrestricted tokens. The priority field in asynchronous frames is a matter of local convention, and implementations should make it tunable for future use. Group (multicast) addresses are defined by the FDDI MAC specification but are not necessarily supported by all hardware; therefore, multicast must not be used for IP and ARP.
sections.plainLanguage: FDDI can use short 16-bit addresses or longer 48-bit addresses, but all computers on the same network must agree on which to use. If you need to mix them, you need a router between them.

sections.title: IEEE 802.2 LLC and Related Standards
sections.content:
All FDDI implementations must support IEEE 802.2 standard Class I service for compliance with the 802.2 standard, even if not strictly required for IP and ARP. This requires supporting Unnumbered Information (UI) Commands, eXchange IDentification (XID) Commands and Responses, and TEST link (TEST) Commands and Responses.

When an XID or TEST command is received, a response must be returned with Destination and Source addresses, and DSAP and SSAP, swapped. The Final bit in the response must be copied from the Poll bit in the command. XID commands have an LLC control field value of 175 (decimal) if the Poll/Final bit is off or 191 if it is on. TEST commands have a control field value of 227 if the Poll/Final bit is off or 243 if it is on. Command frames have the high-order bit of the SSAP reset to zero; response frames have it set to one. XID response frames must include an 802.2 XID Information field of 129.1.0 indicating Class I connectionless service. TEST responses must echo the information field from the corresponding TEST command.
sections.plainLanguage: FDDI must support some extra control messages defined by the IEEE standards, like ping commands and identification requests.
